title: Price Multiplier
context: Grade 4, the multiplying half of the chapter's last section. An adult sees a price multiplied, which looks like long multiplication with a dot in it. What is actually being settled is where the dot goes. The page says to put it at the appropriate place and never says where, and its only multiplication worked in columns comes out to whole rupees. Here the paise column is worked first, as that example does, each hundred paise is carried as one rupee, and the paise left are written as two digits after the dot. The same example prints its multiplier with a dot in front of it, under the paise. The multiplier counts things, so it has no dot and no paise, and this tool has nowhere to put one.

writeup.why: Multiply a price by a count, paise first, put the dot in its place, and follow a cost through to the change or the money left.
writeup.look: A multiplying frame in the middle of the canvas under a row of the things being bought, a carry circle over the rupees, and a two-step card with a change bench at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Price Multiplier' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the things counted against the things in the row, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each thing lights and the second fixed at the number of things drawn. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The thing row runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 90 at 64,214, drawing the things being bought, up to twelve, each dark until it is counted and lit as it is. The multiplying frame stands under it at the left, 540 by 330 at 64,316. Its top line holds the price of one thing in a rupees column and a paise column, with the near-black dotted line between them and the vermilion dot on it, and the headings Rs and p above it outside the working. The second line holds the times sign at the far left and the count box beside it in sky blue, both to the left of the rupees column and outside both columns; the second line has no cell under the paise at all. The counter that fills the count box sits under the frame, 240 by 56 at 64,660, sets whole things only and has no dot key. A carry circle sits over each rupees place. The paise box stands beside the frame, 200 by 110 at 620,316, and the multiply control under it, 200 by 56 at 620,440. Multiply works the paise column first: the paise times the count is written in the paise box as a number of paise, each hundred in it gathers into a full strip that rolls up into one rupee and drops into the carry circle over the rupees, and the paise left go down after the dot as two digits, with a zero in front of fewer than ten. The rupees are then multiplied and the carried rupees added, and the cost is written on the answer line. At the right stand the two-step card, 320 by 110 at 830,316, holding the money a buyer has or pays, and the change bench under it, 320 by 280 at 830,440, which sets the cost under that money in columns with the dots in one line and takes it away. When the paise on top are too few, the bench breaks one rupee into a hundred paise, the rupees figure struck through and rewritten one less above it in amber. The cost stays in a box of its own on the bench while the money left or the change is found. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a dot key, for writing a cost, a change or the money left, and the answer slot prints Rs before the number and holds exactly two places after the dot. The counter that sets the count is not the pad: it has whole numbers only and no dot key. On the fourth phase the slot's label names what the question asks for, the cost, the change or the money left. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. The count is drawn in sky blue in its own box on every phase and is never written in a rupees or a paise column, so nothing on the stage can read it as money. Every answer with paise writes them as two digits after the dot.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last product the child worked, the count in its box with no dot, each carry in its circle, and the answer the question asked for.

phases.win: the hundreds roll up into the carry circle, and the rupees and the carry add into the cost
phases.does: multiplies the paise by the count, rolls each hundred into the carry circle, then multiplies the rupees and adds the carry
phases.goal: money is multiplied paise first, each hundred paise carried as one rupee, and then the rupees
phases.says: Multiply the paise first. How many whole rupees do they make?
phases.check: Away from the screen: one pencil box costs Rs 45.50. What do four cost? Say what the paise made first.
phases.feels: the paise of every thing bought pile up, and every full hundred of them becomes a rupee
phases.hands: Cost a class party list on paper one line at a time. Take one line, six packets of juice at Rs 12.50, and multiply the paise first: fifty paise six times is three hundred paise. Swap the three hundred for three rupee coins on the desk, then multiply the rupees and add the three.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what do the paise make when multiplied? Second rung, the phase's: how many whole rupees is that? Third rung: the frame is cut to one rupee and fifty paise times two, and the child carries before the larger price comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the rupees and the paise look like two separate numbers, and each is given its own product written in full.
wrong.move: multiplies the rupees and the paise apart and writes Rs 138.300, leaving the carried rupees in the paise.
wrong.screen: the paise box shows three hundred paise, and three full strips fill one after another, each rolling up into a rupee and dropping into the carry circle, which reads three. Two zeros go down after the dot in the paise column, the rupees product takes the three, and the child's Rs 138.300 stays in the slot beside the new cost.

wrong.why: the paise look like a small extra on the price, and it is easy to multiply the big part and copy the small part.
wrong.move: multiplies the rupees and brings the fifty paise down unchanged, writing Rs 138.50, as if only the rupees were bought six times.
wrong.screen: the six notebooks in the row light one at a time, and a copy of the price, rupees and paise together, slides down under each. The six lots of fifty paise are counted together in the paise box, three hundred paise, and roll up into three rupees in the carry circle. The rupees product takes them, and the child's Rs 138.50 stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a price on the top line, a count on the second, and the carry circle empty
phases.soWhat: Multiply the paise first, carry each hundred paise as one rupee, then multiply the rupees and add the carry.

phases.win: the count settles in its box with no dot, and the row of things lights one by one to match it
phases.does: counts the things one by one, lifts the count out of the paise column, and sets it in the count box with no dot
phases.goal: the number multiplied by counts things, so it is written without a dot and has no paise
phases.says: What does this number count? Does it have any paise?
phases.check: Write the cost of three kites at Rs 22.40 each as a multiplication. Where does the three go, and does it have a dot?
phases.feels: the number multiplied by is how many things, and things come whole
phases.hands: Write the cost of eight pens at Rs 14.25 as a multiplication on the board, first with the eight under the paise and a dot in front of it, the way the chapter's worked example prints its count. Ask the class what the eight counts, and whether pens can have paise. Then rewrite it with the eight in a box beside the times sign, and multiply.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does this number count? Second rung, the phase's: can a count have paise? Third rung: the row is cut to two things with the count already in its box, and the child multiplies before the larger count comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the chapter's one multiplication worked in columns prints its count that way, and a dot beside a number in a money sum looks like the money's own dot.
wrong.move: copies a layout that puts a dot in front of the nine under the paise, and reads the nine as nine paise.
wrong.screen: the nine pens in the row stay dark while the count stands under the paise. The count is then lifted out: its dot falls away, it settles in the sky blue count box beside the times sign, and the pens light one at a time up to nine. The price is multiplied by the count, and the child's reading stays written in the slot.

wrong.why: with the count standing under the paise, the paise are the only digits it seems to reach.
wrong.move: multiplies only the digits standing over the count, the fifty paise, carries four rupees and writes Rs 18.50, leaving the rupees unmultiplied.
wrong.screen: the count moves into its box beside the times sign, and a near-black bracket reaches from the box across both columns of the price. The paise are multiplied, four hundred and fifty, and the rupees too, one hundred and twenty-six, and with the four carried the cost comes to Rs 130.50. The child's Rs 18.50 stays in the slot beside it.

phases.screen: a frame where the count stands with a dot in front of it under the paise, and a row of the things above
phases.soWhat: The number multiplied by counts things, so it has no dot and no paise.
phases.concept: The number multiplied by is a count

phases.win: the paise left land as two digits after the dot, and the carried rupees join the rupees
phases.does: multiplies the paise, carries the whole rupees, writes the paise left after the dot, then finishes the rupees
phases.goal: when the paise do not come to whole rupees, the paise left are written as two digits after the dot
phases.says: Some paise are left over. Where do they go?
phases.check: One bag of beads costs Rs 21.35. What do seven bags cost? Say what went after the dot.
phases.feels: whatever the hundreds leave behind is still paise, and it still takes two places
phases.hands: Multiply Rs 20.35 by three with the class, paise first: a hundred and five paise. Swap a hundred of them for a rupee coin and ask what is left to write after the dot. Write it with one digit first, Rs 61.5, and ask the class to read it aloud; then write Rs 61.05 and read that.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many paise did the paise make? Second rung, the phase's: how many are left once the whole hundreds are carried? Third rung: the frame is cut to a price with five paise times three, and the child writes the fifteen paise after the dot before the larger price comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: five is one digit and seems to need only one place, and nothing in the multiplying says the paise take two.
wrong.move: writes the five paise left from a hundred and five as one digit after the dot, Rs 49.5 for Rs 49.05.
wrong.screen: the child's Rs 49.5 is read back on the answer line with the second place after the dot empty, which says fifty paise, and fifty cells shade on a strip. A zero is then set in the first place after the dot and the five moves to the second, and the shading falls back to five cells. Both answers stand side by side, the child's still in the slot.

wrong.why: the forty is written after the dot and the rupees look like a separate job, so the rupee in the carry circle is left behind.
wrong.move: forgets the carried rupee and writes Rs 168.40 for four cups at Rs 42.35.
wrong.screen: the carry circle over the rupees glows amber with its one still in it, and the rupees product, one hundred and sixty-eight, is lit beside it. The circle's rupee travels down into the product, making one hundred and sixty-nine, and the child's Rs 168.40 stays in the slot beside the new cost.

phases.screen: a price whose paise times the count is not a whole number of hundreds, with the dot waiting in the answer line
phases.soWhat: The paise left over are written as two digits after the dot, and each whole hundred is carried as a rupee.
phases.concept: Paise left over go after the dot

phases.win: the change or the money left lands in the answer slot, and the cost stays in its box as a step
phases.does: finds the cost by multiplying, sets it under the money held, takes it away, and fills the answer slot
phases.goal: a two-step question finds the cost first and then the change or the money left, which is the answer
phases.says: First find the cost. Is the cost what the question asks for?
phases.check: Four tins of paint cost Rs 72.35 each. How much is left from Rs 300? Say which number is the answer.
phases.feels: the cost is on the way to the answer, not the answer itself
phases.hands: Give each group Rs 500 of play money and a list: three pots of paint at Rs 64.25 each. They find the cost first, then pay it out of the Rs 500 and count what is left. Ask which number the question wanted, and where the cost went once it had been used.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the question ask for? Second rung, the phase's: what is the cost, and what is it taken from? Third rung: the card is cut to one thing bought with one note, and the child finds the change before the larger question comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the multiplying was the long part of the work, and its answer looks like the end of it.
wrong.move: stops at the cost, Rs 593.25, when the question asks how much money is left.
wrong.screen: the child's number is set in the cost box on the bench, where it matches, and the answer slot's label, money left, lights in reddish purple. The cost is then set under Rs 700 on the change bench, a rupee is broken into a hundred paise because there are zero paise on top, and the money left is taken away. The child's Rs 593.25 stays in the slot beside the cost box.

wrong.why: with nothing on top in the paise column, the twenty-five paise below look as if they come straight down.
wrong.move: takes the cost from Rs 700 without breaking a rupee, bringing the twenty-five paise straight down, and writes Rs 107.25.
wrong.screen: the paise cell stays shut over the grey zeros of the Rs 700, and the child's twenty-five is written small beside it. One rupee is broken into a hundred paise, seven hundred struck through and six hundred and ninety-nine written above it, and a hundred less twenty-five gives seventy-five. The rupees then take away, and the child's Rs 107.25 stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a two-step card with the money held, a price and a count, and the answer slot asking for the money left
phases.soWhat: Find the cost first, then answer what the question asks: the cost, the change or the money left.

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the count is lifted out of the paise column. Its dot falls away and rolls off the frame, the count settles into its own sky blue box beside the times sign, and the things in the row light one at a time. As each one lights, a copy of the price card slides down beside the frame, until the copies stand in a stack, one for each thing, and the stack adds up to the same cost the frame gives by multiplying. It can be done as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a price stands on the top line of the frame and a count in its box on the second, with the row of things above lit to match and the carry circle empty. On the second a copied layout lies over the frame, the count standing as a loose card under the paise with a dot in front of it, and the row of things above is dark. On the third the price's paise times the count will not make whole hundreds, and the dot waits on the answer line. On the fourth the two-step card holds the money a buyer has, with the price and the count beside it, and the answer slot asks for the money left. The running count at the top left holds the things counted against the things in the row, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the paise of the price, or the stray dot, or the dot on the answer line, or the two-step card, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the whole row costs. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any price and any count, with the carry circle and the change bench open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on multiplying paise first, writing the count with no dot, writing the paise left after the dot, and two-step questions that end on the change or the money left.
voiceLines: A row of things and the price of one. What does the whole row cost?
Multiply the paise first. How many whole rupees do they make?
What does this number count? Does it have any paise?
Some paise are left over. Where do they go?
First find the cost. Is the cost what the question asks for?
A new price. Count the things before you multiply.
Free play. Any price and any count, with the carry circle and the change bench open.
Multiply the paise again, and watch where each hundred goes.
Every hundred paise carried, every count kept free of a dot, and every question answered as it asked.

observations.why: Every hundred paise in the product is one rupee, so it belongs with the rupees and is added to them.
observations.soWhat: Multiply the paise first, carry each hundred paise as one rupee, then multiply the rupees and add the carry.
observations.observe: The paise times the count rolled up into the carry circle a hundred at a time, and the rupees took the carry.

observations.why: The number multiplied by says how many things there are, and a number of things has no rupees and no paise.
observations.soWhat: The number multiplied by counts things, so it has no dot and no paise.
observations.observe: Once the count was lifted into its own box and lost its dot, the row of things lit one by one to match it.

observations.why: The paise take the two places after the dot, so five paise left over are written with a zero in front.
observations.soWhat: The paise left over are written as two digits after the dot, so five paise are written 05.
observations.observe: When the paise product was not a whole number of hundreds, what was left went after the dot as two digits.

observations.why: The question asked what was left after buying, and the cost is what was taken away to find it.
observations.soWhat: Find the cost first, then answer what the question asks: the cost, the change or the money left.
observations.observe: The cost stayed in its box as a step while the answer slot took the money left.

source_tool.description: A multiplying frame fills the stage under a row of the things being bought. The price of one thing sits on the top line in a rupees column and a paise column, with its dot on a dotted line between them. The number of things is set on the second line from a counter that counts whole things only. The count stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns: the second line has no paise cell and the counter has no dot key, so a count cannot be given paise, and as it is set the things in the row light one at a time. The multiply control works the paise column first. The paise times the count is written in a box as a number of paise; each hundred rolls up as one rupee into a carry circle over the rupees, and the paise left, as two digits, are written after the dot. The rupees are then multiplied and the carried rupees added. On the right, a two-step card holds the money a buyer has or pays, and a change bench takes the cost from it in columns, breaking one rupee into a hundred paise when the paise on top are too few.
source_tool.art_direction: A row of things over one price / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Multiply the paise again, and watch where each hundred goes.
voice.onNext: A new price. Count the things before you multiply.
voice.opening: A row of things and the price of one. What does the whole row cost?
voice.onFinish: Every hundred paise carried, every count kept free of a dot, and every question answered as it asked.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any price and any count, with the carry circle and the change bench open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The number multiplied by is a count
Paise left over go after the dot

placement.where: After a class party list has been costed line by line on paper, and one line's paise have come to more than a hundred. The tool is what rolls every hundred paise up into the rupees and has no place for a dot under the count, which a copied layout on paper does not stop.

answer_key.rule: When each thing costs the same, the cost of several is the price of one multiplied by the number of things. Multiply the paise first. The paise times the count is a number of paise; each hundred of them is carried as one rupee, and the paise left are written as two digits after the dot. Then multiply the rupees and add the rupees carried. The number multiplied by counts things, so it has no dot and no paise, and it is written beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns. Some questions take two steps: find the cost, then take it from the money held or paid, breaking one rupee into a hundred paise if the paise on top are too few. The answer is the one the question asks for, the change or the money left, and the cost is a step.
answer_key.wrong: The count is lifted back out and the row of things counted one at a time, and the paise column is multiplied again with each hundred rolling up into the carry circle in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Paise first: 50 paise times 6 is 300 paise.
300 paise is 3 rupees with no paise left, so write 00 after the dot and carry 3 rupees.
Rupees: 23 times 6 is 138, and the 3 carried make 141. The cost is Rs 141.00, which is Rs 141.
items.question: One notebook costs Rs 23.50. What do 6 notebooks cost?
items.checkpoint: Multiply the paise first, carry each hundred paise as one rupee, then multiply the rupees and add the carry.
items.misconception: Multiplying the rupees and the paise apart and writing Rs 138.300, with the carried rupees left in the paise.

steps: The price of one pen, Rs 14.50, has rupees and paise.
The 9 counts pens, so it is written without a dot, outside the rupees and paise columns.
50 paise times 9 is 450 paise: carry 4 rupees and write 50 after the dot. 14 times 9 is 126, and 4 more make 130, so Rs 130.50.
items.answer: The 9 counts pens, so it has no dot and no paise. The pens cost Rs 130.50
items.question: A child sets out the cost of 9 pens at Rs 14.50 each as 14.50 x .9, with a dot in front of the 9 under the paise. What does the 9 count, and what do the pens cost?
items.checkpoint: The number multiplied by counts things, so it has no dot and no paise.
items.misconception: Copying a layout that puts a dot in front of the count under the paise, and reading the 9 as 9 paise.

steps: Paise first: 35 paise times 4 is 140 paise.
140 paise is 1 rupee and 40 paise. Carry 1 rupee and write 40 after the dot.
Rupees: 42 times 4 is 168, and 1 more makes 169. The cost is Rs 169.40.
items.question: One cup costs Rs 42.35. What do 4 cups cost?
items.checkpoint: The paise left over are written as two digits after the dot, and each whole hundred is carried as a rupee.
items.misconception: Writing all of 140 after the dot, which gives Rs 168.140, or writing 4 after the dot instead of 40.

steps: First the cost: 65 paise times 5 is 325 paise, so carry 3 rupees and write 25 after the dot. 118 times 5 is 590, and 3 more make 593, so Rs 593.25.
Then the money left: Rs 700 is 700.00, and from zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 699 and 100 paise.
100 less 25 is 75 paise, and 699 less 593 is 106. Rs 106.75 is left, and the cost was a step.
items.question: A child has Rs 700 and buys 5 bags of rice at Rs 118.65 each. How much money is left?
items.checkpoint: Find the cost, then take it from the money held, and answer what the question asks.
items.misconception: Stopping at the cost, Rs 593.25, when the question asks for the money left.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: One pencil costs Rs 7.50. What do 4 pencils cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 30. 50 paise times 4 is 200 paise, which is 2 rupees, and 7 times 4 is 28, so 28 and 2 make 30

items.question: One ribbon costs Rs 12.25. What do 4 ribbons cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 49. 25 paise times 4 is 100 paise, which is 1 rupee, and 12 times 4 is 48, so 48 and 1 make 49

items.question: Rs 26.40 is multiplied by 3 to find what 3 books cost. Is the 3 written with a dot in front of it?
items.final_answer: No. The 3 counts books, so it has no dot and no paise. The books cost Rs 79.20

items.question: A child writes the cost of 7 bottles at Rs 31.20 each as 31.20 x .7 and reads the .7 as 70 paise. What should the 7 be, and what do the bottles cost?
items.final_answer: The 7 counts bottles, so it has no dot and no paise. 7 times Rs 31.20 is Rs 218.40

items.question: One torch costs Rs 85.60. What do 3 torches cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 256.80. 60 paise times 3 is 180 paise: carry 1 rupee and write 80 after the dot. 85 times 3 is 255, and 1 more makes 256

items.question: One ball costs Rs 16.35. What do 3 balls cost?
items.final_answer: Rs 49.05. 35 paise times 3 is 105 paise: carry 1 rupee and write 05 after the dot, because the paise take two places. 16 times 3 is 48, and 1 more makes 49

items.question: A child buys 6 boxes of crayons at Rs 64.75 each and pays with a Rs 500 note. How much change comes back?
items.final_answer: Rs 111.50. The crayons cost Rs 388.50, and Rs 500 less Rs 388.50 is Rs 111.50. The question asks for the change, not the cost

items.question: A child has Rs 450 and is given Rs 300 more, then buys 4 lamps at Rs 162.80 each. How much money is left?
items.final_answer: Rs 98.80. The child has Rs 750 and the lamps cost Rs 651.20. From zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 749 and 100 paise, so Rs 98.80 is left

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the price of one thing in a rupees column and a paise column
draws the things along the top and lights one for each counted
sets the number of things, whole things only, with no dot key
works the paise column first, then the rupees
shows the paise times the count before anything is carried
takes one rupee for each hundred paise
holds the money held or paid in a two-step question
takes the cost from that money in columns

teaching_notes: Cost a class party list line by line on paper before the tool is opened, and make sure one line's paise come to more than a hundred. Then use the tool for where the dot goes. The page says to put it at the appropriate place and never says where, and its one multiplication worked in columns, eight pencils at eighteen rupees fifty paise, comes out to whole rupees, so it cannot show paise left over. Work the paise column first, as that example does: carry each hundred paise as one rupee, and write the paise left as two digits after the dot. Two exercise questions leave paise over, so the case is not rare. The same example prints the eight with a dot in front of it, under the paise. Say plainly that the eight counts pencils, so it has no dot and no paise, and write it outside the rupees and paise columns. Two exercise questions go on to ask for the change or the money left, so the cost is a step in both, and the second takes paise from zero paise by breaking a rupee into a hundred paise. It also says a sum was taken without saying from where; read it as money added to what was already held.
generation_prompt: Build a money multiplying tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A row of the things being bought is drawn along the top of the working area. Below it a multiplying frame holds the price of one thing on its top line, in a rupees column and a paise column with the dot on a dotted line between them. The number of things is set on the second line from a counter that counts whole things only and has no dot key; the count stands in a box of its own beside a times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, and that line has no paise cell, so a dot can never be placed under the paise. As the count is set, the things in the row light one at a time. A multiply control works the paise column first and shows the paise times the count in a box; each hundred rolls up as one rupee into a carry circle over the rupees column, and the paise left are written as two digits after the dot. The rupees are multiplied next and the carry added. At the right, a two-step card holds the money a buyer has or pays, and a change bench sets the cost under it in columns and takes it away, breaking one rupee into a hundred paise when the paise on top are too few. An answer slot names what the question asks for, the cost, the change or the money left. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Multiply the paise first. Carry each hundred paise as one rupee. Write the paise left after the dot. The count has no dot. Then find the change or the money left.
